text: This week, at a dinner in Washington, DC, House Majority Leader Tom DeLay      said, `We now live in a right-of-center nation.'  But how close is the      United States to returning the Republican Party to the commanding      influence it enjoyed a hundred years ago in the days of William McKinley      and Theodore Roosevelt?  Historian Lewis Gould is the author of "Grand      Old Party:  A History of the Republicans."  He's at member station KUT in      Austin, Texas.
Welcome.
Thank you.
And Republican strategist and pollster David Winston joins      us here in the Washington studio.
And thank you for being with us.
Glad to be here.
Now, Mr. Winston, let's start with you.  How far away do you      think the Republican Party is from the kind of majority it wants to have?

Well, I think what you saw in the 2004 election was an      emerging framework, that you could see the party has an opportunity to      create a long-term majority.  It is not there, and there are things that      still need to be accomplished.  Again, Bush only won by a couple of      points.  It wasn't like some second terms--like, FDR in his second term      won by a huge margin; Nixon in his second term won by a huge margin.      Bush won by a couple points, and it's: What does the Republican Party do      to govern over the next couple of years to then be able to achieve that?

And I would actually argue with Congressman DeLay.  We are not a      right-center country; we're a center-right country.  And because of that      slight lean to the right, there's this opportunity for the party.
Professor Gould, how do you think the strength of the      Republican Party today compares with its dominance in the early part of      the 20th century?

Well, after Theodore Roosevelt won election in 1904, he got      56 percent of the vote to 37 percent for the Democrats, so that was a      real blowout over Alton B. Parker.  The Republicans had about 60 votes in      the Senate, which they wish they had right now, and they had a dominant      majority in the House.  So it was, in that way, much more of a Republican      nation in 1904 than it is now.  I would agree with the characterization      of the center-right.

Well, talk about the difference between the party today in      terms of geography and demography and what it stands for, and how that      differs from the Republican Party--the turn-of-the-century party.

Well, if you looked at a map of the election of 1900, an      electoral map, and the map of 2000, it would look as though George Bush      was William Jennings Bryan and Al Gore was William McKinley, because in      1900, the South was solid for the Democrats.  There was literally,      virtually, no Republican vote that was counted anywhere in the old      Confederacy.  And their strength was in the upper Midwest and the      Northeast, with some bitterly contested states in the Middle West like      Illinois and Ohio.  So it was very much a party of the Northeast and the      North, and the Democrats were a party of the South and the West.  Now      it's quite the opposite.
David Winston, immigration was a big boon for the Democrats      in the last century, and now there's an area where the Republican Party      has made gains and expects to make more gains.
And has made significant gains.
In fact, the president was up by--What?--9 points with      Hispanic voters in the last election over previous performances.

In 2000, he was at 35 percent; in 2004, he was at 44      percent. But the Hispanic community is a very diverse community.  You      have at least three very clear groups of Hispanics in this country.  You      have Puerto Ricans, predominantly in the Northeast; Cubans in northern      New Jersey and down in Florida; and then you have Mexicans, but also      Central American as well.  They are three very distinct communities.  The      one thing that does tend to pull them together is Catholicism.  Catholics      in this country, since Reagan at least, have been a critical swing vote,      and the Hispanic community is tending to follow that tradition.

Lewis Gould, looking back again, voters cooled to the GOP.      As the Depression set in, the party came to represent something remote      and indifferent and rich in the minds of many voters.  Do you think that      the party has completely shaken that?

I do think that it has tempered its image as the party of      big business over the last 50 or 60 years, largely on cultural issues, so      that somewhat incongruous or sometimes discordant parts of the country      coexist with each other for different reasons.  In the 1880s and 1890s,      there was a very powerful evangelical thrust within the party, which      produced a backlash in the election of 1890, and the Republicans tempered      their identification with evangelicals after that into the early 20th      century.  I guess David could speak more to the power and thrust of the      evangelicals in the party and what that bodes for the future than I can.
Go ahead, David.

As you begin to develop a majority coalition, inevitably      what that means is there are more people coming into your coalition.  The      more interests that you have within that coalition, the more stress you      develop. And that's ultimately why coalitions eventually do fall apart,      because you can't manage those fissures and that stress.  And so you have      a range of people, for example, within the Senate, of everybody from      Chafee in Rhode Island to a Brownback in Kansas.  And as Frist, I'm sure,      deals with, that's a pretty wide range of political ideology to manage on      a day-by-day basis.
Let me ask each of you where you see future successes.      David Winston.

I do think that the success that the Republicans had in      this last election with Hispanics is going to continue.  Immigrants are      coming to this country for opportunity.  Within a lot of surveys, you see      that that's a strength of the party, the sense of opportunity and      optimism in terms of the economic outlooks.  So with Hispanics, the one      opportunity.
Lewis Gould, what do you think?

Well, I think resolving the potential split between      evangelicals and, as David points out, the Roman Catholics--because      they've held together on such issues as abortion and gay marriage, but      the evangelical agenda, which at least as I hear it either explicitly or      implicitly has some problems for Roman Catholics, is not going to be an      easy balance to sustain into the future.  There's only one...
The kind of thing you're talking about would be?

Their sense of what should be taught in the public schools.      On an issue like evolution, which the Catholic Church has no opposition,      per se, to evolution, evangelicals are very much against the teaching of      evolution; that would be a potential flash point.  But also, evangelicals      are, in much of their rhetoric, anti-Catholic.  They do not believe that      the pope is a legitimate representation of Christianity.  And as these      tensions come to the fore--they've been sublimated and submerged--there's      a potential for denominational conflict that would work against the      long-range interests of the Republicans.
Historian Lewis Gould is the author of "Grand Old Party:  A      History of the Republicans."  David Winston is a Republican pollster and      strategist.
Gentlemen, thank you both very, very much.
Thanks for having us.
Thank you for having me.
Next week, how the future looks for Democrats.
It's 18 minutes past the hour.
From NPR News, this is NEWS & NOTES. I'm Tony Cox, in for Farai Chideya.

President Bush will try to win over a tough American audience tonight when he delivers the State of the Union address. It will not be easy. Polls show the majority of voters do not favor the president's leadership. The number one reason: the war in Iraq.

Consider the latest Washington Post-ABC News survey, for example. The report says Americans overwhelmingly oppose Bush's call to send an additional 21,500 troops to the region. So what will it take for the president to regain public support? And how might voters line up on domestic issues like health care, immigration and education?
We have asked two political strategists to help us take a preliminary look at this evening's State of the Union address and share more about what voters are thinking as we approach election 2008.
Republican pollster David Winston is at NPR headquarters in Washington D.C. He leads the Winston Group, a political research firm in the nation's capital.
David, nice to have you.

speaker_label: Mr. DAVID WINSTON (Republican Pollster; Director, Winston Group)
text: I'm glad to be here.

And national pollster Silas Lee is on the line from New Orleans, Louisiana. He is a sociology professor at Xavier University and heads Silas Lee and Associates, a polling agency based in the Crescent City.
Silas, nice to have you as well.

speaker_label: Professor SILAS LEE (Sociology, Xavier University; Political Pollster; Director, Silas Lee and Associates)
text: Thank you very much. Good to talk with you.

Let's begin here. David, I'm going to come to you, because with the - and let's also start with the biggest issue, which, as we mentioned, is Iraq. Major polls are showing that the president is at the weakest point of his presidency. So how difficult will it be for the president to pull himself out of this slump? And number two, how far can a speech - albeit an important one - go toward accomplishing that for the president?

speaker_label: Mr. DAVID WINSTON (Republican Pollster; Director, Winston Group)
text: Let me do that in reverse order. A speech can be enormously effective if it does the right thing in terms of inspiring people. Again, going back to the president's speech right after 9/11, that clearly shaped and defined who he was at that point in time and obviously got direction he was looking for.

speaker_label: Mr. DAVID WINSTON (Republican Pollster; Director, Winston Group)
text: This is going to be a difficult speech. The war has not gone at all the way the administration had defined it. He's trying to change the strategy. And there is as equally a lack of confidence at this point shown in the election and in his particular ability to lead at this point. So he's got to stand up and show some clear direction and get people to sort of buy back into his leadership. And that's a pretty tough thing to do. It's imminently doable, but it's tough.
I incorrectly said that you are at NPR headquarters in Washington. We know that you're on the phone. Just wanted to get that straight before I continue.

speaker_label: Mr. DAVID WINSTON (Republican Pollster; Director, Winston Group)
text: Okay.

Silas, let me ask you a question, because as we've already said, confidence in the president's leadership continues to suffer largely because of the war. Now, polls can differ, of course, but from your point of view, what are the keys for the president tonight?

speaker_label: Professor SILAS LEE (Sociology, Xavier University; Political Pollster; Director, Silas Lee and Associates)
text: Well, keep in mind with the State of the Union, usually it's a menu in terms of presenting a lot of alternatives to voters. And naturally - here's the problem for the president right now as was mentioned earlier, President Bush basically mortgaged his presidency to a large degree on the war. And that was after the 9/11 attack.

speaker_label: Professor SILAS LEE (Sociology, Xavier University; Political Pollster; Director, Silas Lee and Associates)
text: And then now, he's almost attempting to refinance it almost to gaining more support in terms of increasing the number of troops with the war. The problem is like was mentioned - a loss of confidence. Overwhelmingly, voters feel that we need to go to another direction. And a recent poll I saw indicated that the majority of people would like Congress to take the lead on issues. So this speech is a prelude - people would like to see action and agenda, a plan.

speaker_label: Professor SILAS LEE (Sociology, Xavier University; Political Pollster; Director, Silas Lee and Associates)
text: And in terms of gaining confidence with the public - that's an incremental process. And that's something you build on after you have accomplished some initiative. So naturally, for the president, he will have to try to gain confidence with people definitely in reference to some of the domestic issues.

speaker_label: Professor SILAS LEE (Sociology, Xavier University; Political Pollster; Director, Silas Lee and Associates)
text: Energy - I'm quite sure - he's going to highlight, as well as education, health care reform, research and medical science. All those are going to be very broad-brushed issues he will address. However, again, it will take time to gain confidence, and you do not gain confidence immediately from a speech. It's like being in a marriage, and one partner happens to stray. Then it takes time to rebuild that trust and confidence in that situation. Same here.

One of the things that it would seem to me, David, is that for the president to regain the confidence of the people, he would have to convince the people that he is paying attention to what their needs and wishes are. To what extent do you think that the Bush administration has taken and will continue to take public sentiment to heart?

speaker_label: Mr. DAVID WINSTON (Republican Pollster; Director, Winston Group)
text: Well, I think one of the things you saw is the president's reaction to this election in terms of clearly a need for change in strategy. Changing the secretary of defense was obviously a big step. And also, really, understanding that he's going to have to communicate what his goals and objectives in Iraq were, but laying it out in such a way that people could follow. That's, obviously, one of the primary elements of the speech.

speaker_label: Mr. DAVID WINSTON (Republican Pollster; Director, Winston Group)
text: The other element is - as was being said - is there's a focused on domestic policy, dealing with cost-of-living issues such as health care, education and getting into energy. And you're going to see some focus here, obviously, on ethanol-based - increasing ethanol-based fuels, his proposal in terms of health care, to make it more accessible to individuals. You're going to see a domestic focus here, as well as the Iraq situation.

speaker_label: Mr. DAVID WINSTON (Republican Pollster; Director, Winston Group)
text: But I agree. This is going to be a first step, but this is an important dynamic in that he needs to engage people here at this point because we're about to get into the next presidential race. And for him to sustain his ability to drive an agenda, he has to do well this evening.

Silas, we've had you on the program before, mostly to give us a rundown on what's going in New Orleans politically, but your research does extend beyond that area and goes all the way to Capitol Hill. Let me ask you about the African-American electorate. Has dissatisfaction among African-Americans about this president's agenda been pretty much the same or has it changed? And to what extent are black voters in sync with American voters overall, particularly when it comes to the president's strategy on the war?

speaker_label: Professor SILAS LEE (Sociology, Xavier University; Political Pollster; Director, Silas Lee and Associates)
text: Well, definitely, in answer to your question, yes. Black voters are in sync on several issues. For example, decline in support for the president. Keep in mind, his support among black voters wasn't that high to begin with. And since the ongoing problems with the war in Iraq, it has deteriorated somewhat.

speaker_label: Professor SILAS LEE (Sociology, Xavier University; Political Pollster; Director, Silas Lee and Associates)
text: Also, in reference to addressing the critical issues - education, public safety, health care reforms. All those are critical issues where the president, he has scored low with black voters and he hasn't necessarily changed with black voters in terms of addressing those issues.

speaker_label: Professor SILAS LEE (Sociology, Xavier University; Political Pollster; Director, Silas Lee and Associates)
text: And let me make a point, too. After 9/11, President Bush was in a very strong position, whereby he could take the platform and play the role of a coach and say that this is what we need to do, and people would basically fall in line, lockstep. Since the war, that has changed. And not just since the war, but since the problems with the war in terms of the casualties and the strategy to get out of the war. People are looking for some level of compassion, someone they feel that is listening and responsive to them and not so entrenched in a belief that they feel is wrong.

speaker_label: Professor SILAS LEE (Sociology, Xavier University; Political Pollster; Director, Silas Lee and Associates)
text: So that is going to be a challenge whereby the president must be able to convince people that he is listening - not only listening, but responding, and not just taking a position that this is what I'm going to do and the polls don't matter, as he said it in the past.

Well, David, we've identified you as a Republican pollster, and along the lines of the black electorate, we know that the Republicans reached out at the last presidential election with some degree of success.
Do you see that - how do you see the black electorate playing into the overall strategy of the White House with regard to trying to win back the public's support?

speaker_label: Mr. DAVID WINSTON (Republican Pollster; Director, Winston Group)
text: Well, I mean, that's long term - and this is sort of stating the obvious - there's obviously been a frustration in both directions in terms of African-Americans being frustrated with the Republican Party and the Republican Party being frustrated that there couldn't be more progress made in the African-American community.

speaker_label: Mr. DAVID WINSTON (Republican Pollster; Director, Winston Group)
text: Having said that, that had been one of the focal points in terms of No Child Left Behind, the education initiative, thinking that that was a particular policy that, in fact, would have some impact. I would actually disagree. Republicans have not made much progress from 2000 forward in terms of (unintelligible) at the presidential level around 8 or 9 percent, and pretty much stayed at that level.

speaker_label: Mr. DAVID WINSTON (Republican Pollster; Director, Winston Group)
text: You had a situation with Michael Steele running in Maryland, an African-American, who got 25 percent of the African-American vote in Maryland. And that's one of the better performances that you've seen in terms of any Republican.

speaker_label: Mr. DAVID WINSTON (Republican Pollster; Director, Winston Group)
text: It's critical in terms of if we want to regain a majority coalition that we're going to have to pick up minority voters. And so in terms of the long term success of the party, there has to be some successful outreach here.
Let me bring our conversation to a close with this final question for the both of you. First to you, Silas, and briefly: what would you not want to hear from the president tonight?

speaker_label: Professor SILAS LEE (Sociology, Xavier University; Political Pollster; Director, Silas Lee and Associates)
text: Definitely, I would not want to, you know, quite a few many people would not want to hear a strong focus on being entrenched in a particular ideology. And that's the main thing people would not want to hear. This is what I believe. There needs to be a greater emphasis on responding to the needs and the concerns of the American people.

speaker_label: Professor SILAS LEE (Sociology, Xavier University; Political Pollster; Director, Silas Lee and Associates)
text: And quite often people - mea culpa works effectively, where you admit that, look, we have had some shortfalls, and maybe we need to rethink our position. And this is how we want to engage in some corrective action. So maybe those are strategies that would be effective in this speech.
Same thing to you, David. We have just about a minute left. What would you be most concerned about and not want to hear from the president?

speaker_label: Mr. DAVID WINSTON (Republican Pollster; Director, Winston Group)
text: Well, I'm actually going to be similar in my answer. You want to hear a focus on solutions and how is he going to address and solve people's problems, not how he's going to promote an ideology. And I think there's one concern - and you've seen this in some polls - the sense of stubbornness on his part and not willing to listen.

speaker_label: Mr. DAVID WINSTON (Republican Pollster; Director, Winston Group)
text: And one of the things that you want to see in this speech is that he's listened, he's focused on solutions and solving people's problems. That would be a good transition and could potentially set him up so he could sustain driving the agenda for the next two years. And we'll see if he can do it.

I appreciate your time, gentlemen. Republican strategist David Winston is president and founder of The Winston Group. He joined us by phone. And national pollster Silas Lee is a professor of sociology at Xavier University. He heads Silas Lee and Associates. And he joined us by phone from New Orleans. Gentlemen, thank you.

speaker_label: Professor SILAS LEE (Sociology, Xavier University; Political Pollster; Director, Silas Lee and Associates)
text: Thank you.

speaker_label: Mr. DAVID WINSTON (Republican Pollster; Director, Winston Group)
text: Thank you.
Just ahead, nuclear power gets an energy boost. And TV, is it better or worse?

So how does a national hero run against to man who has now become a figure in American history?  Very carefully. David Winston is a Republican strategist who advised former speaker Newt Gingrich and former Senator William Frist, among others.  He joins us in our studios.  Mr. Winston, thanks so much for being with us.
Glad to be here.
Americans generally - all across the political spectrum, seem to be proud that this milestone...  ..TEXT: Mr. WINSTON:  Ahah...
Of Senator Obama's nomination has been achieved in American history.  Is there some hazard - do you have to take particular care in criticizing Senator Obama in a certain way?

In terms of talking about issues, no problem.  And the fact is he did something big - acknowledge it,  just as Obama has done in terms of talking about John McCain's experiences as a P.O.W. He's clearly acknowledged it and then sort of pivots off - but we do have some disagreements. To some degree, McCain's got to learn how to do the same thing now talking about Obama.
Any issues that are promising for him?

Well, certainly.  I mean, he starts off with having some strength in terms of national security issues. But the number one issue facing this country, I would expect that the biggest area of debate that we're going to watch between the two candidates is the economy. And as a key sub-element of that, obviously, gas prices.

John McCain's got to come up with exactly what he's going to be for. You're watching Obama start to develop his now that he gets out of the primary, and I don't think at this point it's clear who's going to have the upper hand.  The one thing that McCain does have that is going to prove to be a challenge to Obama is he does have some access to independents that perhaps other Republican candidates don't.  Inversely, you have Obama having access to younger voters and sort of more well-to-do affluent voters.

And so you're looking at a situation that I think is particularly interesting, that maybe in perhaps previous elections, where the Republican candidate had access to maybe 52 percent, the Democrat 51, so there was no middle.  Both of these folks have access to maybe 60, 65 percent of the electorate. And so it's a very different election.
In your judgment, should Senator McCain say anything about race?
Now, you realize a lot of people are just going to hear that long pause.

Well, because it's a very complicated question, and there was a long pause there. I mean, there's a historic achievement here.  So that is a positive step forward for the entire country that I think the entire country sees.

But in another level, what that's also saying is that Barack Obama has gotten this country beyond race at a certain level.  And so do you want to bring up something that in essence could be conflictive with the event that just happened?  My personal suggestion to him would be stick to issues. Appreciate Barack Obama's achievement in sort of being the first African-American presidential candidate. Bbut this country wants to know where the economy is going, and what we're going to do in Iraq.
Senator McCain has recently been kidding himself publicly about age.  Is this a patter he should keep up?
My guess is you'll see his mother quite a bit on the campaign trail as a...
Whose age...

Who's in her 90s and is pretty boisterous for 95, as an example of the gene pool that he comes from, so he's physically fine.  But I think that's a sort of entertaining and pleasant way for the American people to sort of hear him discuss age in a way that sort of takes some of the tension of that discussion now.
Will Senator McCain's selection for vice president - does it diffuse either the race or age issue?

From my personal point of view, he needs to have someone on the ticket not from a regional wing of ideology point of view.  I think what he needs is someone who has got significant credibility in terms of the economy, and that it would be a significant help to him.
David Winston is a Republican strategist.  Thanks so much for being with us.
Pleasure.
Congress returns this week with a vote to repeal the nation's health care law. While the measure will pass, the Republican-controlled House, it won't make it through the Democratic-controlled Senate.

Our next guest advises the Republican leadership in both the House and the Senate. Republican pollster David Winston spent the weekend at the House GOP's retreat in Baltimore and he joined us in our studio.
Good morning.
Good morning.

Recent polls are showing that support and opposition to the law remain just about equally divided  the health care law. Aside from the fact that fulfilling a Republican campaign promise is important, what is the strategy in continuing with this vote?
Well, first off, I would suggest that actually some of the polls have shown the margin a little bit wider. Generally, it's either neutral or has been slightly negative toward the law.

With the strategy here is, is one, it was a campaign promise but the other dynamic is Republicans feel that this is an important debate to have and so the idea is let's get it through the House and then we can get into the debate with the Senate and the president in terms of, so, what should this look like?
And the tone of the debate?
I think you're going to see the tone of the debate be exactly the way John Boehner said it would when he came in as speaker, when he said we can disagree without being disagreeable.
John Boehner, though, has actually changed a little bit of the language already - what had been referred to by Republicans as a job-killing bill is now being referred to in a slightly different way.
I think he's describing it as job-destroying.
I mean, subtle but different.

No. And, again, this gets to who he is. Look, was he has to have and he understands that both sides are going to have very strong positions and they need to be able to debate those positions. I would suggest to you the Republicans won the political debate on health care...
And the election.
...and - and the election - and so therefore with the dynamic that John Boehner's trying to set up is saying, Okay, here's our position, let's have a debate about where we should go.
There has been quite a chorus from Republican leaders to the effect that the Democrats still control Washington. What is the thinking with that? It sounds like lowering expectations.

It's setting up and understanding what the realistic situation. Look, Democrats still have significant control over the process by having the Senate and the White House. And so understanding that as we try to move forward, this is going to be a very difficult process.

Now, haven't said that, the challenge to both the Republicans and Democrats is people want to see something done. And if there's a perception that one side is playing politics - and I'm not saying which one; I'm just saying if it's perceived - that will be a negative for that particular side.

On the other hand, there are many voters - and I'll say in the Tea Party - who are quite passionate about getting very dramatic things done and who were the big part of the Republican win. Might that be a problem for Republicans?

No. I think in talking to Tea Party members what you find is, yes, Tea Party members have some very clear beliefs but they also want to see progress made. And they also sense there's this sense of responsibility. So, for example, when you talk about increasing the debt ceiling, there's an understanding that we have to maintain our obligations in terms of our financial commitments.

But having said that, there's an expectation that there are going to be some additional items within that that will move this country more towards fiscal responsibility. And so it's the sense of don't simply just acquiesce but you have to maintain your obligations as well and so how do you effectively balance that?
As a Republican strategist, what do you see as the major pitfalls, the dangers for Republicans going forward in trying to achieve their agenda under complicated circumstances?

Let me start at a much broader level, and I would suggest this isn't necessarily the problem Republicans face; it's every speaker. This is the same problem Nancy Pelosi had, Dennis Hastert, Newt Gingrich, Jim Wright. I mean, just go back over time. And that is you're managing a majority coalition; you've got a lot of members who don't necessarily agree on everything.

Now, one of the things I will tell you that is John Boehner's strength is the ability to get everybody pointed in the right direction. It's one of the singularly most difficult thing for leaders to do. It is one of his key strengths. It is also one of his key challenges.
Republican pollster David Winston advises Republican leaders in the House and the Senate. Thank you very much for joining us.
Thanks for having me.
You're listening to MORNING EDITION from NPR News.
